meta.document: No county appropriation — Middlesex County government was abolished in 1997
meta.title: Middlesex County — the money that remains
meta.note: Massachusetts abolished Middlesex County government in 1997. There is no county budget, no county council, and no county judge. The county-level public money that remains flows two ways — the Middlesex Sheriff's Office, funded by the Commonwealth through the state budget, and the Registries of Deeds, funded by recording fees. The budgets that shape daily life here — police, schools, roads, trash — are set by the cities and towns and by the state, not by the county. This page shows the county-level money that still exists; everything else is a dead end here only until it's ingested from the city, town, and state sources.

nodes.name: Middlesex County appropriation
nodes.note: There is no county appropriation. Middlesex County government was abolished on July 11, 1997; its functions passed to the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. A dead end means "not yet ingested and navigable" — here it means the thing itself no longer exists at the county level, which is the honest answer.

nodes.name: Middlesex Sheriff's Office (state-funded)
nodes.note: The Sheriff's Office runs the county jail and house of correction and is funded by the Commonwealth through the annual state budget (line item around 8910). The exact appropriation will be ingested from the Massachusetts state budget and CTHRU — the one real county-level budget number for Middlesex.

nodes.name: Registries of Deeds (fee-funded)
nodes.note: The Middlesex North (Lowell) and South (Cambridge) Registries of Deeds record property transactions and are funded by the fees they collect. Their revenue and operating figures will be ingested from the Commonwealth's records.
